Order of the imaging studies relative to the craniotomy is not stated (the abstract lists the craniotomy before the investigation).
The intervention text says spasticity was treated with inhibitory techniques, but the patient's own tone findings are flaccidity and hypotonia; spasticity is not documented as a separate finding.
The date of the admission is given only as "in July" and the interval "after two years" has no clear anchor; no year is stated.

Skin-care and some oral facilitation sentences are worded as general statements ("can enhance tone", "is used") rather than documented care of this patient; the Phase II vibration and manipulation sentence is not recorded.

A Glasgow Coma Scale of 7 (severe) is reported in the same paragraph that says the patient was oriented to time, place and people; the source does not reconcile or time these findings.
Table 1 "Day 7" and the text "On day 7" (tone assessment, Table 2) are not stated to count from the same reference point.
"the same condition" follows a sentence about hypertension medicine; it is read as stroke because it repeats "affected by" from the previous-stroke sentence, but the referent is not named.

claims.text: A 45-year-old woman with hypertension, treated with medicine for two years, and two previous strokes treated with medical and physiotherapy treatment was admitted in July with flaccidity of the right upper and lower limbs and very challenging bed mobility. She had no sensory issues or deformities, was oriented, scored GCS 7, NIHSS 30 and mRS 5, had hampered bowel and bladder function and was on intermittent catheterization, with a Ryle’s tube for feeding.

claims.text: She underwent a decompressive craniotomy and, after 36 hours of ICU monitoring, was shifted to the surgery ward. A rehabilitation program was planned and treatment began after surgery. Phase I (day 1 to four weeks) used Rood’s facilitation, inhibitory techniques, passive movement of the right upper limb, bed mobility exercises and oral facial facilitation; Phase II (four to eight weeks) included PNF, breathing exercises and oral motor drills.

evidence.quote: In this case, she underwent a decompressive craniotomy.
The patient underwent a decompressive craniotomy.

An approach-oriented rehabilitation program was planned for the patient.

Phase I (day 1 to four weeks): Roods method - facilitating treatments used for treating flaccidity in the right upper limb include quick brushing, quick icing of the muscular bellies, tapping, and performing severe joint compression.

Spasticity was treated with upper limb inhibitory techniques such as slow stroking and rolling, prolonged stretching, pressure on the muscle insertion, light joint compression, and unresisted contractions.
On the patient, passive movement of the right upper limb was performed, as shown in Figure 2.
The patient was instructed in bed mobility exercises for supine to side lying, such as logrolling and segmental rolling with additional support.
Oral facial facilitation helped with swallowing frequency control, sensory awareness, and motor control.

Phase II (four to eight weeks): Roods Method - fast brushing, quick icing of the muscular bellies, tapping, and severe joint compression are facilitative treatments for relieving flaccidity in the lower limbs.

Spasticity was treated with upper limb inhibitory techniques such as soft stroking and rolling, prolonged stretching, pressure on the muscle insertion, mild joint compression, and unresisted contractions.
The proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF) technique was used to improve the physical functioning of the patient (Figure 3).
It was practiced as often as the patient can during the day in between each round of breathing exercises.
Inhaling via the mouth and exhaling through a pursed lip are two of these breathing exercises.
Oral motor sensory drills were done to improve deglutition, tongue movement, and lip closure when chewing and slurring.

claims.text: Pretreatment and posttreatment scores were NIHSS 30/42 and 12/42, mRS 5/6 and 1/6, FIM 70/126 and 95/126, Brunnstrom upper and lower limb stage 1 and stage 5, and voluntary control Grade 0 and Grade 2. The authors describe the interventions as very effective, with a good recovery rate that improved quality of life and strength.
